newsitem.title: FRANCE: NEW AIRBUS A330 MODEL MAKES MAIDEN FLIGHT.
newsitem.headline: NEW AIRBUS A330 MODEL MAKES MAIDEN FLIGHT.

text.p: The new Airbus A330-200 twinjet took off on its first test flight on Wednesday, carrying the European consortium's latest offensive against the newly-merged U.S. rival Boeing Co in the world airline market.

Airbus Industrie faces stiffer competition following last month's merger between Boeing and McDonnell Douglas to make a Goliath with annual sales of $48 billion in commercial and military aircraft and space activities.

The A330-200, launched in November 1995 and costing $450 million to develop, directly attacks the Boeing 767 family, Airbus senior vice president commercial John Leahy said, after reporters watched the plane take off at 0930 GMT from an Aerospatiale facility in Toulouse, southwest France.
The four-nation Airbus grouping believes it will sell between 500 and 600 of the new planes over the next 20 years, at a catalogue price of around $110 million, Leahy said.
Airbus had already received a total 132 orders and commitments for the A330-200 even before its first flight and "maybe we will revise upwards our estimate," Leahy said.
Airbus vice president for marketing Colin Stuart said the A330-200 will fly further, faster and carry more passengers and freight than Boeing's 767-300 and 767-400 aircraft.
"We are not interested in being a niche player," Stewart said. "We are intent on being on equal terms with Boeing in the market place".
Airbus aims to win "consistently at least 50 percent of the the market," he added. The consortium expects to hold half the world market by 2003.

The new plane allows airlines to fly non-stop long-haul routes economically, with fewer passengers and increased cargoes. These so-called "long, thin routes," make it unprofitable to fly frequent services using larger aircraft.

Leahy told Reuters an expected doubling of air travel in the next 20 years will mean increased demand for direct flights between secondary national airports such as Toulouse, or Manchester in northern England, as well as growth of the so-called superhubs, such as Paris, London and New York.

The A330-200 will meet the need for those regular, direct flights, so passengers do not need to travel to a big hub and suffer the delays of congestion and crowding. The test plane can fly non-stop from Toulouse to Los Angeles or Bangkok.

Besides competing with the Boeing 767, Airbus hopes to sell the A330-200 as a replacement for the vast fleet of McDonnell Douglas DC10s and Lockheed L1011s in service, as well as the first generation of Airbus A300s and A310s sold since the 1970s.

Tour operators, including Monarch Airlines of Britain, are interested as it allows profitable operations in the winter holiday season when holidaymakers have to fly further to chase the sun but the numbers are lower than in the peak summer period.
First delivery of an A330-200 is due in April 1998 to charter operator Canada 3000, which is leasing the plane from U.S. leasing company ILFC.
Airbus is also attacking Boeing at the upper ranges, with a $2.5 billion programme for variants of its A340 four-engine, long-range plane, launched commercially in June at the Paris air show.
The stretched A340-600 will seat 378 passengers, while the A340-500 will fly 8,500 miles, bringing pressure to bear on Boeing's 777 twinjet and 747 jumbo jet.

Airbus announced orders and commitments for these planes from Virgin Atlantic of Britain and Air Canada on the same day that the Boeing and McDonnell Douglas merger deal was completed at the end of July.
Airbus officials said the timing of the announcements was coincidental.

Leahy said he was confident Airbus would formally launch its high-capacity A3XX plane by the end of 1998, and that risk-sharing partners from Asia, Europe and North America would have signed up by then. The plane will seat between 500 and 700 passengers and could smash Boeing's 747 monopoly of the 400-seater market.
The A3XX, which will cost at least $8 billion to develop, will be Airbus' "flagship for the 21st century," Stuart said.

The A330-200 seats 253 passengers in three classes and flies up to 6,450 miles (12,000 km) at about Mach 0.82. It is a shorter version of the basic A330-300, which seats 295 passengers in three classes and flies 7,300 miles.

Airbus is selling the plane with engines from three major manufacturers, the CF6-80E1 from General Electric, PW4000 from Pratt & Whitney, a subsidiary of United Technologies Corp, and the Trent 700 from Britain's Rolls-Royce Plc. REUTER
